prompt: A LOBSTER plot shows -COHP for a metal-oxygen pair, with a large peak on the negative side just below the Fermi level. What does that peak mean?

options.text: Filled antibonding states, which weaken that bond
options.why: -COHP is positive for bonding and negative for antibonding, so a negative peak below the Fermi level is occupied antibonding character.

options.text: Strong bonding states
options.why: Tempting if you read COHP itself, where bonding is negative; the plot shows -COHP, which flips the sign.

options.text: Empty states that do not matter
options.why: States below the Fermi level are occupied, so they do count.

options.text: A failed projection
options.why: Antibonding peaks are physical; the projection quality is judged by the charge spilling, not by the sign of a peak.

hints: Which sign of -COHP means bonding?
Are states below the Fermi level filled or empty?

prompt: Which VASP settings does a LOBSTER run need from the static calculation before it?

options.text: NSW = 0, ISYM = 0 or -1, LWAVE = .TRUE. and NBANDS at least the number of local basis functions
options.why: LOBSTER reads the WAVECAR, needs the k-points that symmetry would fold away, and needs at least one band per basis orbital to project onto.

options.text: The default ISYM and LWAVE = .FALSE.
options.why: Without a WAVECAR LOBSTER has nothing to project, and a symmetry-reduced mesh lacks k-points it needs.

options.text: ISYM = 2 and LORBIT = 11
options.why: LORBIT writes VASP's own projections; LOBSTER does its own projection from the wavefunctions and needs symmetry off.

options.text: Ultrasoft potentials for speed
options.why: LOBSTER works with PAW potentials only.

hints: Which file does LOBSTER read?

options.text: The second is stronger because its number is closer to zero
options.why: Bonding COHP is negative, so the more negative integral is the stronger bond.

options.text: The first bond has a dissociation energy of 2.1 eV
options.why: ICOHP is not a bond energy that can be measured; it is a basis-dependent indicator.

options.text: Nothing, ICOHP has no meaning
options.why: It is a useful trend indicator, as long as the bonds are compared within one consistent calculation.

prompt: lobsterout reports a large charge spilling. What does that tell you?

options.text: The local basis misses part of the density, so the COHP picture may be incomplete
options.why: The spilling is the fraction of the density the projection fails to reproduce; a large value means a poor fit of the basis to the states.

options.text: The SCF did not converge
options.why: The spilling measures the projection, not the VASP electronic loop.

options.text: The bonds are very ionic
options.why: Ionicity is a property of the material; the spilling is a property of the projection.

options.text: Too many k-points were used
options.why: More k-points do not cause spilling; the basis does.

hints: What is projected onto what?

prompt: Why are Wannier functions not unique, and how do maximally localized Wannier functions fix the choice?

options.text: Each Bloch state has a free phase (and bands can be mixed); MLWFs pick the mixing that minimizes the total spread
options.why: The gauge leaves every band energy unchanged but reshapes the Wannier functions; Marzari and Vanderbilt choose the gauge with the smallest spread.

options.text: Because the DFT energies are uncertain
options.why: The ambiguity exists even for exact Bloch states; it is a phase freedom, not a numerical error.

options.text: They are unique; any code gives the same functions
options.why: Without a localization criterion the functions depend on the arbitrary phases, so they are not unique.

options.text: MLWFs fix it by choosing the most extended functions
options.why: The criterion is the opposite: the smallest spread.

hints: What happens to a Bloch state if you multiply it by a phase?
What does maximally localized minimize?

visual.caption: From Bloch states to Wannier functions.
visual.alt: A three-step flow: Bloch states from a DFT run, a choice of phases and mixings, a Fourier transform to real space.

prompt: The d bands you want to wannierize cross several s bands. Which step of Wannier90 handles that?

options.text: Disentanglement, with an outer window and a frozen inner window
options.why: Souza, Marzari and Vanderbilt pick the best subspace of the right size from the outer window at each k, keeping the frozen-window states exactly.

options.text: Raising num_iter
options.why: More iterations help the localization converge, but they do not separate entangled bands.

options.text: Turning symmetry on
options.why: Symmetry reduces the k-mesh, which Wannier90 cannot use; it does not disentangle bands.

options.text: Using fewer bands in VASP than Wannier functions
options.why: You need at least as many bands as Wannier functions, and usually more, to disentangle.

hints: What is special about bands that cross other bands?
Which two energy windows does Wannier90 use?

visual.caption: The Wannier90 steps for entangled bands.
visual.alt: A four-step flow: set the outer energy window, set the frozen window, disentangle, then localize.

prompt: After a Wannier90 run, what is the most direct check that the model is right?

options.text: The Wannier-interpolated bands lie on the DFT bands inside the frozen window
options.why: The model's job is to reproduce the bands it came from; plotting both together shows any mismatch at once.

options.text: The spread is smaller than in the last run
options.why: A small spread is good, but a localized model can still reproduce the wrong bands.

options.text: The run finished without errors
options.why: Finishing says nothing about whether the bands agree.

options.text: The number of Wannier functions equals the number of atoms
options.why: The count follows the chosen orbitals (for example eight sp3 functions for two Si atoms), not the atoms.

hints: What should a tight-binding model reproduce?
Where must the agreement be exact?

visual.caption: Checking a Wannier model.
visual.alt: A three-step flow: compute the DFT bands, run Wannier90, overlay the interpolated bands on the DFT bands.

prompt: Why does the VASP run for Wannier90 switch symmetry off?

options.text: Wannier90 needs the overlaps between neighbouring points of the full uniform k-mesh
options.why: The spread is computed from overlaps between each k-point and its neighbours on a uniform mesh, which a symmetry-reduced list does not contain.

options.text: Symmetry makes the bands wrong
options.why: Symmetry does not change the bands; it removes k-points from the list.

options.text: To make the run faster
options.why: Switching symmetry off makes the run slower, not faster.

options.text: Because Wannier functions only exist in triclinic cells
options.why: Wannier functions exist for any crystal; the issue is the k-point list.

hints: What does Wannier90 compute from neighbouring k-points?
What does symmetry do to the k-point list?
